items.title: Roll20 Data Breach: Attacker Got Password Hashes Through an Image-Upload Flaw
items.summary: Roll20, the online tabletop where millions play D&D and other role-playing games, says an attacker reached a database of account information through a flaw in its image uploads. Affected players started getting the warning email on Friday, 20 November. The first posted about it on Bluesky around 17:50 UTC. At 18:37 UTC, Chief Technology Officer Mike Todd confirmed the incident in a post on Roll20’s forum . The attack happened on the evening of 16 November. Fewer than 1% of Roll20’s users were affected, Todd wrote, and every one of them got an email. If you didn’t, Roll20 says your account wasn’t involved. For those who did, the data includes names, email addresses and bcrypt hashes of their passwords. A smaller group with a saved payment card also had the card’s last four digits exposed. When we published, the story was on Bluesky and Roll20’s own forum. We found no news coverage.

items.title: CVE-2026-23871: WhatsApp Bug Helped Scammers Make Messages Look Legitimate
items.summary: WhatsApp patched three security flaws, including one exploited in a real scam campaign to make fraudulent messages appear more credible. WhatsApp’s November security advisory fixes three flaws, including CVE-2026-23871, a vulnerability in Click to WhatsApp ads affecting WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4. “Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread.” reads the advisory. “This issue may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.” The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker. SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible. “Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek. The second fix is more serious on paper, though WhatsApp has seen no sign it was ever used. CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection on WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74, triggered when someone taps a specially crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client. “A SQL injection vulnerability when the recipient tapped on a specially crafted “order details” message from an unofficial client in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 could have allowed deletion of locally-stored WhatsApp files and, only if the user is online at time of receipt, leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user’s chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing sidechannel.” continues the report. The company is not aware of attacks in the wild exploiting this flaw. The third, CVE-2026-44908, lives deeper in WhatsApp’s infrastructure than in the app itself. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that confirms trust with Meta AI’s confidential computing backend, across WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business on iOS, Android and Mac. Someone positioned inside Meta’s own infrastructure could, in theory, have presented a certificate signed by the wrong key to bypass the hardware root of trust, but such a certificate would first need to appear on a public transparency ledger, and WhatsApp says that ledger shows every published certificate checks out clean. These issues come after two fixes released in May. One addressed a bug in Instagram Reels message handling that could make another person’s device load media from an attacker-controlled URL. The other fixed a Windows attachment-spoofing trick. By adding a NUL byte to a filename, an attacker could make an executable file look like a normal document. Meta received reports of both flaws through its bug bounty program, and there is no evidence that attackers exploited them. Of the three new flaws, only one was used in a real-world scam. It also had the lowest technical impact. This shows that scammers don’t always need to exploit serious vulnerabilities or gain access to a device. A convincing message can be enough to deceive a victim. Make sure you update WhatsApp on all your devices. The fixed versions vary across iOS, Android, Mac, Windows and WhatsApp Business. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-23871)

The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker.

SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

“Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The company is not aware of attacks in the wild exploiting this flaw.

The third, CVE-2026-44908, lives deeper in WhatsApp’s infrastructure than in the app itself. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that confirms trust with Meta AI’s confidential computing backend, across WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business on iOS, Android and Mac. Someone positioned inside Meta’s own infrastructure could, in theory, have presented a certificate signed by the wrong key to bypass the hardware root of trust, but such a certificate would first need to appear on a public transparency ledger, and WhatsApp says that ledger shows every published certificate checks out clean.

items.title: A Vulnerability in VMware Products Could Allow for Authentication Bypass
items.summary: A vulnerability has been discovered in VMware vCenter, which could allow for authentication bypass. VMware vCenter Server is a centralized management platform used to administer VMware vSphere environments, including ESXi hosts and the virtual machines running on them. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. Depending on the privileges associated with the account, an attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights. Accounts configured to have fewer user rights on the system could be less impacted than those that operate with administrative user rights.

items.title: 1984 Hosting Hacked: Iceland’s Privacy-First Web Host Shuts Down Every Service
items.summary: 1984 Hosting, the Icelandic web host that sells itself on privacy and free speech, has switched off everything it runs after a cyberattack. The company announced the shutdown on Friday, 20 November, around 11:00 UTC, in a joint statement with CERT-IS , Iceland’s national cybersecurity incident team. It calls the attack well planned and technically sophisticated. Email and DNS are meant to come back first, under close monitoring. Web hosting, VPS servers and the rest stay off until security checks are finished, and 1984 can’t yet say when that will be. The statement doesn’t say whether customer data was taken. One customer says it was. The operator of Wagyu, a Monero swap service, blames the breach for a $13.5 million theft of his wrapped Monero token earlier the same day. When we published, Icelandic media and crypto news sites had the story. English-language security outlets didn’t yet.

items.title: Healthcare Sector Disclosed 100 Ransomware Attacks in Q3
items.summary: Ransomware groups are running riot, with 353 disclosed attacks in Q3 2026 and 2,668 undisclosed attacks, an increase of 20% in disclosed attacks and an increase of 77% in undisclosed attacks from Q3 2025, according to the Q3 2026 State of Ransomware Report from BlackFog . More attacks were disclosed in Q3 2026 than in any other quarter since BlackFog began tracking ransomware attacks in 2020, and each month in Q3 had more disclosed attacks than any Q3 month in previous years. Across all industry sectors, there were 123 disclosed attacks in July, 116 in August, and 114 in September. Healthcare topped the list with 100 disclosed attacks in the quarter, followed by government (41), services (38), Technology (30), and manufacturing (28). Disclosed attacks only account for a small percentage of total attacks. Factor in claims of attacks on data leak sites, and the picture changes considerably. For undisclosed attacks, services topped the list (575 claimed attacks), followed by manufacturing (548), and technology (294), with healthcare in fourth spot with 239 claimed attacks. Combined, that places healthcare in third place with 339 attacks in the quarter. Out of all disclosed attacks, 98% involved data exfiltration, and in one-third of attacks the group responsible could not be determined. The biggest ransom demand – $13 million – came from the ShinyHunters attack on the U.S. data center operator CyrusOne, with an average ransom demand across Q3 of $763,253. BlackFog reports that, on average, 697 GB of data was exfiltrated per victim, with the most common payment deadline of just 3 days. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Data exfiltration occurs in the vast majority of attacks, and since data breaches require individual notifications in healthcare under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, victims of healthcare ransomware attacks should be informed if their data is stolen, but that’s certainly not the case with other sectors. Across all sectors, only 1 in 9 ransomware attacks is publicly disclosed. For most victims, they are not notified, there is no announcement, and they may be totally unaware that their data has been leaked on a dark web data leak site. In terms of confirmed data breaches, the ransomware attack on Saber Healthcare Group was the most impactful of the quarter, involving the personal and health information of a confirmed 282,727 individuals. Saber Healthcare did not disclose the group responsible, and it was not added to any data leak site, which could indicate that the ransom was paid. In Q3, there were 116 active ransomware groups, with 21 new ransomware groups emerging, although two groups dominate the ransomware landscape – The Gentlemen and Qilin. BlackFog reports that both groups tied with 347 entries each on data leak sites in Q3. The Gentlemen operation has rapidly scaled, with a massive increase in attacks, helped by the group’s ability to attract new affiliates with a 90% share of ransoms paid, compared to a more typical 70-80% by other groups, and a full attack toolkit available to affiliates. The two groups accounted for 26% of all leak site activity in the quarter. The United States remained the most targeted country, accounting for 53% of disclosed attacks and 39% of undisclosed attacks.

More attacks were disclosed in Q3 2026 than in any other quarter since BlackFog began tracking ransomware attacks in 2020, and each month in Q3 had more disclosed attacks than any Q3 month in previous years.

Across all industry sectors, there were 123 disclosed attacks in July, 116 in August, and 114 in September. Healthcare topped the list with 100 disclosed attacks in the quarter, followed by government (41), services (38), Technology (30), and manufacturing (28).

Disclosed attacks only account for a small percentage of total attacks. Factor in claims of attacks on data leak sites, and the picture changes considerably. For undisclosed attacks, services topped the list (575 claimed attacks), followed by manufacturing (548), and technology (294), with healthcare in fourth spot with 239 claimed attacks. Combined, that places healthcare in third place with 339 attacks in the quarter.

Out of all disclosed attacks, 98% involved data exfiltration, and in one-third of attacks the group responsible could not be determined. The biggest ransom demand – $13 million – came from the ShinyHunters attack on the U.S. data center operator CyrusOne, with an average ransom demand across Q3 of $763,253. BlackFog reports that, on average, 697 GB of data was exfiltrated per victim, with the most common payment deadline of just 3 days.

Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy

Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy

Data exfiltration occurs in the vast majority of attacks, and since data breaches require individual notifications in healthcare under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, victims of healthcare ransomware attacks should be informed if their data is stolen, but that’s certainly not the case with other sectors. Across all sectors, only 1 in 9 ransomware attacks is publicly disclosed. For most victims, they are not notified, there is no announcement, and they may be totally unaware that their data has been leaked on a dark web data leak site.

In terms of confirmed data breaches, the ransomware attack on Saber Healthcare Group was the most impactful of the quarter, involving the personal and health information of a confirmed 282,727 individuals. Saber Healthcare did not disclose the group responsible, and it was not added to any data leak site, which could indicate that the ransom was paid.

In Q3, there were 116 active ransomware groups, with 21 new ransomware groups emerging, although two groups dominate the ransomware landscape – The Gentlemen and Qilin. BlackFog reports that both groups tied with 347 entries each on data leak sites in Q3. The Gentlemen operation has rapidly scaled, with a massive increase in attacks, helped by the group’s ability to attract new affiliates with a 90% share of ransoms paid, compared to a more typical 70-80% by other groups, and a full attack toolkit available to affiliates. The two groups accounted for 26% of all leak site activity in the quarter. The United States remained the most targeted country, accounting for 53% of disclosed attacks and 39% of undisclosed attacks.

The frequency of recent incidents increases risks for commercial shipping, particularly vessels transiting near Iranian-controlled waters. items.title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims
items.summary: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information. The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems. The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers. JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses. “Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly. The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring. Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed. Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational. The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies. The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees. The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations. Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed. Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention. For this reason, third-party risk management needs to go beyond contractual security requirements and periodic questionnaires. JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information.

The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems.

The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers.

JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses.

“Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring.

Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed.

Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational.

The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies.

The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees.

The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations.

Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed.

Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention.

Organizations should know what information suppliers can access, limit the data they share, review access privileges and require timely incident reporting. They should also verify that providers apply appropriate security controls and have effective procedures to detect and contain intrusions.

items.title: Vulnerabilities OFFIS DCMTK Toolkit Can Result in Data Deletion
items.summary: Two more vulnerabilities have been identified in the OFFIS DCMTK toolkit that could result in the deletion of medical imaging data. The most serious vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125130 and has a CVSS v3.1 severity score of 9.1. The vulnerability is due to a read-only archive area accepting network stores. Each unauthorized store can trigger the archive’s own quota cleanup, which would delete existing studies, potentially resulting in total data deletion from the archive. The vulnerability can be exploited by a network peer without credentials. The vulnerabilities were identified by security researcher Abhinav Agarwal, who demonstrated in tests on DCMTK 3.7.0 that the server accepted 200 unauthorized stores, triggering the archive cleanup resulting in the deletion of 200 original synthetic image files. The final query confirmed that all 200 original image files had been deleted. Agarwal determined that while DCMTK enforced read-only access, that only occurred when a connection was set up. “If a peer asked to use the storage service on a read-only area, the server refused. It still accepted the Verification service (DICOM “echo”), which is harmless by itself,” explained Agarwal. “Once connected, however, the server executed whatever command arrived without checking that it matched the service negotiated for that connection. A peer could negotiate Verification only and then send storage commands over it.” Data deletion occurs when the read-only area is full, resulting in the deletion of the least recent imaging data to provide space for the most recent store. The second vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-126500 and has a CVSS v3.1 score of 5.9 (medium severity). The vulnerability is due to the cleanup process deleting studies by prefix, rather than using exact matching. “To evict a study, cleanup picks the oldest one, then deletes every index record whose Study Instance UID starts with the selected UID,” said Agarwal. “Study selection elsewhere in the same backend uses exact matching. Cleanup did not.” Agarwal demonstrated in tests that evicting the study ending .1 also deleted the studies ending .10–.19 and .100–.199 – resulting in 111 studies deleted in a single eviction. Data deletion could occur without any attacker involvement and could result in data loss from unrelated studies. Agarwal also uncovered five unrelated vulnerabilities in the same toolkit earlier this year, which have since been fixed. The latest two vulnerabilities were reported to the developer and CISA and affect versions 3.5.4 to 3.7.0. The developer fixed both vulnerabilities in DCMTK version 3.7.1, which was released on October 15, 2026. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy While the new version fixes the vulnerabilities, they may still be present in products that incorporate the DCMTK archive server, including certain Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora package sources. “An SBOM line that says ‘DCMTK’ doesn’t answer the question. Hospitals and suppliers need to know whether the archive server or its backend is in the build, which revision it came from, and whether both fixes made it downstream”, said Agarwal.”

items.title: Yuma Regional Medical Center Pays $1,985,000 to Settle Data Breach Lawsuit
items.summary: Yuma Regional Medical Center, a 406-bed general and teaching hospital in Yuma, Arizona, that now operates as Onvida Health, has agreed to settle class action litigation stemming from an April 2022 cybersecurity incident. Hackers accessed its computer systems between April 21, 2022, and April 25, 2022, and used ransomware to encrypt files . Prior to encryption, the ransomware group exfiltrated files containing patient information, including names, Social Security numbers, health insurance information, and limited medical information. The data breach was reported to the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights as involving the protected health information of 738,145 individuals. Court documents suggest that notification letters were mailed to 720,217 current and former patients. Multiple class action lawsuits were filed in response to the data breach. The lawsuits asserted similar claims and were consolidated into a single complaint with 13 named plaintiffs. The consolidated lawsuit – Dillon Clarke, et al. v. Yuma Regional Medical Center – is pending in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona. The consolidated complaint alleges Yuma Regional Medical Center was at fault for the data breach, as it failed to ensure the privacy and security of data in its possession. The lawsuit claimed it failed to implement appropriate cybersecurity measures, failed to detect the incident until the attackers made contact and explained that data had been stolen, and then failed to issue timely notification letters to the affected individuals. The lawsuit asserted claims for negligence, breach of implied contract/implied duty of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty, and violation of the Arizona Consumer Fraud Act. Yuma Regional Medical Center denies the claims and contentions in the lawsuit, including the allegations of wrongdoing and liability. During mediation, all parties were able to reach an agreement on suitable settlement terms, thereby avoiding the cost of continued litigation and the risks associated with a trial and related appeals. Under the terms of the settlement, Yuma Regional Medical Center has agreed to establish a $1,985,000 settlement fund to pay benefits to class members after attorneys’ fees and expenses, settlement administration costs, and service awards for the class representatives have been deducted. Class members may submit a claim for reimbursement of documented, unreimbursed out-of-pocket losses incurred due to the data breach between April 21, 2022, and February 1, 2027, up to a maximum of $4,000 per class member. In addition, class members are entitled to claim a pro rata cash payment, which will be paid from the remaining settlement funds. The amount will be determined by the number of claims received. All class members will also automatically receive one year of medical data monitoring services. Yuma Regional Medical Center has already invested, or will invest more than $750,000 in data security measures to better protect patient data. Individuals wishing to opt out of the settlement must do so by January 4, 2026. Objections must be filed by the same date, and claims must be submitted by February 1, 2027. The final fairness hearing has been scheduled for March 1, 2027. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy

Corrective action plans typically last two years and require the organization to complete a risk analysis, put a risk management plan in place, update policies and train staff, all under OCR monitoring. That work has to be done anyway. Doing it before an investigation is far cheaper and less disruptive than doing it after one.

When the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) investigates a healthcare provider, one of the first documents it asks to see is the Security Risk Analysis. For most practices, that is where the trouble starts.

At OCR’s cybersecurity conference earlier this year, senior OCR officials returned to the same point again and again: most organizations they investigate cannot provide a compliant risk analysis. [Insert attributed quote: speaker name, title, exact wording]. In OCR’s view, a practice without an accurate and thorough risk analysis cannot be HIPAA compliant, because every other security decision depends on it.

This is not a new problem, and it is not limited to large health systems. The good news is that a compliant risk analysis does not need to be a burden on a busy practice. This article explains what the Security Risk Analysis is, what OCR expects to see, why so many practices fall short, and how to complete yours quickly with the right tool.

What OCR found when it looked

The clearest evidence comes from OCR’s own audit program. In 2016 and 2017, OCR audited 166 HIPAA-covered entities and 41 business associates. Its industry report found that only 14% of covered entities had substantially fulfilled the requirement to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis. Put another way, 86% fell short.

Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy

Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy

The results for the next step were worse. Only 6% of covered entities adequately implemented risk management, which is the process of acting on what the risk analysis finds.

Those audits are several years old, but OCR’s comments this year suggest little has changed. The risk analysis remains the most commonly cited failure in OCR’s enforcement actions, and OCR has built a dedicated enforcement program around it.

Why the Security Risk Analysis is the foundation of HIPAA compliance

The HIPAA Security Rule requires covered entities to “conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability” of the electronic protected health information (ePHI) they hold (45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)).

The Security Rule is deliberately flexible. It does not tell a three-doctor family practice to use the same safeguards as a 500-bed hospital. Instead, it asks each organization to decide which safeguards are “reasonable and appropriate” for its own size, systems and risks. That flexibility only works if you know what your risks are.

That is why the risk analysis comes first. It tells you:

  • Where ePHI lives in your practice, and who and what can access it.
  • Which threats are realistic for you, from phishing and ransomware to a lost laptop or an unlocked records room.
  • Which of your current safeguards are working, and where the gaps are.
  • Which risks matter most, so you spend time and money in the right places.

Your policies, staff training, access controls, backup plans and vendor agreements should all follow from it. Without a risk analysis, a practice is making security decisions without a map.

What an “accurate and thorough” risk analysis covers

OCR’s guidance on risk analysis sets out what it expects to see. A compliant SRA should:
Cover all ePHI, wherever it is created, received, stored or sent: your EHR, practice management system, email, laptops, phones, tablets, backups, cloud services and systems run by vendors.
Identify realistic threats and vulnerabilities, including human error, cyberattacks, equipment failure and natural events.
Assess your current security measures and whether they are being used properly.
Estimate the likelihood and impact of each threat, and assign a risk level.
Be documented, with the analysis kept for at least six years.
Be reviewed and updated regularly, and whenever something significant changes, such as a new EHR, a new location or a security incident.
It also needs to look across the three types of safeguard in the Security Rule:
Safeguard Examples of what the SRA looks at
Administrative Security officer responsibilities, staff training, access approval, sanctions policy, incident response, contingency planning, business associate agreements
Physical Facility access, workstation placement and use, device and media disposal, protection of servers and paper records
Technical Unique user logins, automatic logoff, encryption, audit logs, multi-factor authentication, secure email and messaging, backups

A generic template downloaded from the internet rarely meets this standard, because it does not describe your practice, your systems or your risks. OCR has made clear that a “check the box” document is not an accurate and thorough analysis.
The cost of getting it wrong
In 2024, OCR launched its Risk Analysis Initiative, an enforcement program aimed specifically at organizations that have not carried out a compliant risk analysis. By July 2026, it had produced 14 enforcement actions, and risk analysis failures also feature in many of OCR’s ransomware settlements.
Recent examples show that size is no protection:
Top of the World Ranch Treatment Center agreed to pay $103,000 and adopt a two-year corrective action plan after a phishing attack exposed the ePHI of 1,980 people. OCR found the organization had not conducted an accurate and thorough risk analysis.
BST & Co. CPAs, an accounting firm acting as a business associate, paid $175,000 after a ransomware attack. Again, OCR cited the failure to conduct a risk analysis.
Financial penalties are only part of the cost. Corrective action plans typically last two years and require the organization to complete a risk analysis, put a risk management plan in place, update policies and train staff, all under OCR monitoring. That work has to be done anyway. Doing it before an investigation is far cheaper and less disruptive than doing it after one.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization
items.summary: Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks. Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public. “A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory . An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used. The vulnerability is caused by persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with access to these cookies could connect to the database service and send specific RPC commands, potentially executing arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected device. Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” The attackers used custom Python scripts to scan networks, find accessible SMB resources, connect to SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories. Their goal was to steal credentials and other sensitive information. F6’s analysts think AI tools helped write those scripts, judging by the comments and fix descriptions left inside them, which is a strange kind of courtesy from an intruder. F6 published indicators tied to the activity: two IP addresses, a telltale “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log on affected devices, and Python scripts staged under a specific disk path. “One of the key indicators of successful exploitation is the appearance of a nodeup ‘wombat@127.0.0.1’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.” states F6. “Such an entry indicates that a connection was established with an Erlang node whose identifier corresponds to the known exploitation mechanism — CVE-2026-76466. When such events are detected, organizations should review other logs and artifacts to confirm whether compromise has occurred.” Nobody has linked the attack to a known group yet, so treat this as an active technique without a named author. If you run Expressway, update now, hunt for those indicators, and don’t assume a clean edge device means a clean network behind it. items.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: Trump’s First Move After the Outages: Fire the Cyber Director
items.summary: Trump fired his national cyber director days after outages hit Microsoft, US flights, and the NSA’s classified network. No link to a cyberattack confirmed. The White House fired national cyber director Sean Cairncross, a person close to the administration told Reuters. It’s the first major personnel move since a string of tech failures hit the country over the past week. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will take the role temporarily. The week brought several major disruptions. A global Microsoft outage affected Outlook and Microsoft 365, disrupting services for hundreds of millions of users. A nationwide ground stop also affected more than 18,000 flights. Then, on November 17, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, also went down . CNN reported that six sources confirmed the outage and that some staff at Fort Meade were told to arrive at different times. Three separate systems experienced major disruptions in less than two weeks, raising questions about what was happening. A Defense Department official said the NSA outage followed routine maintenance and caused a “temporary degradation.” Sources told CNN there was no evidence of a cyberattack. A former senior NSA official explained that NSANet is made up of several interconnected networks with built-in redundancy, making a complete outage unusual. However, by midweek, the agency had not said when all services would be restored. “The dismissal of Cairncross is the ​administration’s first major personnel move since the outages. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal ​government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.” Reuters reports . “The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” a person, ​who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters. Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive before taking the cyber director job, said in a statement it had been the honor of a lifetime to serve. It is important to highlight that nobody has linked these outages to each other or to a foreign actor, at least not officially. “The top US intelligence official ​said on Wednesday the disruptions ​were separate ⁠service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Reuters continues. Cybersecurity experts told Reuters separately that the outages are more likely linked to companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities that AI tools now surface faster than before. This is a plausible explanation, even if it is less appealing than blaming a foreign attacker. Finding vulnerabilities faster means companies need to release security updates more quickly. But faster updates also increase the risk of errors that can disrupt services. A series of outages caused by security measures moving too fast may not make dramatic headlines, but it highlights an important lesson: updates must be properly tested before deployment, even when there is pressure to act quickly. Not everyone in Washington is satisfied with that account. Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said this week the administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can tell the public what’s actually happening. “His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.” Reuters concludes. It’s the first major personnel move since a string of tech failures hit the country over the past week. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will take the role temporarily.

The week brought several major disruptions. A global Microsoft outage affected Outlook and Microsoft 365, disrupting services for hundreds of millions of users. A nationwide ground stop also affected more than 18,000 flights. Then, on November 17, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, also went down. CNN reported that six sources confirmed the outage and that some staff at Fort Meade were told to arrive at different times.

Three separate systems experienced major disruptions in less than two weeks, raising questions about what was happening. A Defense Department official said the NSA outage followed routine maintenance and caused a “temporary degradation.” Sources told CNN there was no evidence of a cyberattack. A former senior NSA official explained that NSANet is made up of several interconnected networks with built-in redundancy, making a complete outage unusual. However, by midweek, the agency had not said when all services would be restored.

“The dismissal of Cairncross is the ​administration’s first major personnel move since the outages. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal ​government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.” Reuters reports.

“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” a person, ​who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive before taking the cyber director job, said in a statement it had been the honor of a lifetime to serve.

It is important to highlight that nobody has linked these outages to each other or to a foreign actor, at least not officially.

“The top US intelligence official ​said on Wednesday the disruptions ​were separate ⁠service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Reuters continues.

Cybersecurity experts told Reuters separately that the outages are more likely linked to companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities that AI tools now surface faster than before.


This is a plausible explanation, even if it is less appealing than blaming a foreign attacker. Finding vulnerabilities faster means companies need to release security updates more quickly. But faster updates also increase the risk of errors that can disrupt services. A series of outages caused by security measures moving too fast may not make dramatic headlines, but it highlights an important lesson: updates must be properly tested before deployment, even when there is pressure to act quickly.

Not everyone in Washington is satisfied with that account. Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said this week the administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can tell the public what’s actually happening.

“His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.” Reuters concludes.

items.title: Careers360 Leak Exposes 3.6 Million Indian Students’ Exam Ranks and Caste Categories
items.summary: Data allegedly taken from Careers360, one of India’s biggest exam and college-admission sites, is on a hacking forum. It ties students’ names and phone numbers to their caste category and their entrance exam ranks. Have I Been Pwned , the breach-notification service run by Troy Hunt, loaded the data on Friday, 20 November, at 03:44 UTC. It counts 22 million records with 3.6 million unique email addresses, plus names, phone numbers, genders and caste categories. Most records also hold the student’s entrance exam results, ranks and marks included. The service marks the breach as verified and attributes it to a forum user called 888. The data went up around 14 November, when dark-web monitoring accounts first flagged it. Careers360 hasn’t said anything in public. When we published, the leak was known only from Have I Been Pwned, Hunt’s post about it and those monitoring accounts. We found no press coverage.

items.title: Hunt.io Uncovers Russian-Speaking Credential Theft Operation Targeting US Banks and Government Accounts
items.summary: Hunt.io uncovered a credential-stealing operation that compromised 603 PCs and exposed bank, government and password manager accounts. Hunt.io found an exposed open directory sitting on a Netherlands VPS, and inside it was the live loot store of a credential-theft operation. The report describes decrypted password-manager vaults, cleartext bank logins, and accounts behind the federal identity gateways ID.me and Login.gov. No bank or agency was breached directly; this all happened on the victims’ own Windows PCs. The attackers used three custom-built tools to manage the operation. HavoX handled communication with infected computers and ran commands, Phantom53 managed victims and tasks, while the Kraken Bridge connected the system to an external control panel. HavoX used encrypted connections and hidden Python scripts to operate quietly. Phantom53 tracked infected devices, while Kraken Bridge sent commands and delivered tasks through temporary download links that were deleted after use. The operation affected 603 computers, which had been communicating with three command-and-control systems since October 12. In just three weeks, they generated more than 1.2 million connections. At least 57 victims had US bank or government login details stored on their computers, while 46 had accounts linked to federal benefits or identity services. In one case, the attacker cracked an entire LastPass vault offline, recovering 2,880 logins, including access to a bank account, the IRS and the vault’s own sharing key. The attacker also bypassed Chrome’s newer app-bound encryption by using hardcoded AES-GCM keys for Chrome versions 20 and 21. A script then searched stolen cookies for 28 valuable online services, including Google, Anthropic, Binance, PayPal and several banks. “Across 16 identified victims, the recovered data contained at least 3,345 decrypted login records from Chrome and Edge databases spanning 15 hosts, including plaintext passwords.” reads the report . “The operators also collected 30 cookie database files and JSON cookie exports from multiple victims.” Password managers fared no better. LastPass fell to a custom seven-script pipeline that cracked its AES-CBC storage format and pulled 2,880 logins from one vault alone, plus 17 passkeys and secure notes covering Wi-Fi passwords and security answers. 1Password’s master password was cracked for two victims through a PBKDF2, HKDF, and AES-GCM keyset attack, and a developer’s live KeePass database was lifted straight off a GoLand workstation while the app was still open. Microsoft 365 took a different hit. Stolen ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT session cookies let the operator replay a PKCE OAuth flow and pull live Graph API tokens without ever triggering a login or MFA prompt. Two tenants were confirmed compromised this way, and a reconnaissance log showed the operator mapping accounts and installed software on a corporate host. The attackers also targeted more than banks and email accounts. Four PowerShell scripts stole session tokens from 35 AI developer tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. They also collected credential files, chat histories and API keys. Three other scripts targeted 44 cryptocurrency platforms and seven browser wallet extensions, stealing 6,570 records from 67 victims. To maintain access to infected computers, the operator used legitimate remote-access tools, including ConnectWise ScreenConnect and Level.io. The Level.io installer was built into the attack platform, allowing the attackers to keep access even after the original malware was removed. The operator had developed the platform from the ground, and the custom tooling shows it. The attribution rests on the operator’s own files. Comments, logs, and docstrings across 249 files are written in Russian, in the kind of casual, private language someone uses when they don’t expect anyone else to read it, from a bridge component’s runtime log to section comments inside a seed-phrase search script. Hunt.io’s defensive advice centers on treating AI CLI credential files the same as SSH keys, enforcing conditional access tied to device state, and alerting on pythonw.exe spawning from unusual locations. None of the affected institutions were hacked, which is itself the point the researchers want understood. “None of these institutions is breached. What is exposed is live customer access, which is account-takeover fuel.” concludes the report. “The fix sits on the account side: phishing-resistant authentication, session and device binding, and fast resets for the customers in this loot.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Credential Theft Operation)

items.title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
items.summary: Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community. In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. “I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month. Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI) , rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions. “I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added . These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems. Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility. The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail . Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked. Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis , told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards. “We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.” The math at stake Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics: Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers) Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc. “What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO. Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science. “The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.” 2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance. “A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026 , and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained. AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978). “The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added. Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.” Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen. The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis. Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’ Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis. Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded. Q-Day and LLMs Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography. “We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.” Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use. “We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”

Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis.

Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded.

Q-Day and LLMs

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography.

“We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.”

Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use.

“We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”

items.title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
items.summary: The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them. Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets. “Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush , Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post . “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.” Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025. WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository , and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take. The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address. This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained. Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request. The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors . Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over. But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do. Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.” Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge. They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets. There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work. Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’ Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability , safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com , github.com , or raw.githubusercontent.com . Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.” Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs. “The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.” He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.” Scripts are a soft spot The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.” This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets. And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source. “The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said. Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go? Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said. Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”

items.title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
items.summary: Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems. The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days. “As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.” During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.” Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.” In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.” ARTEX popular with attackers The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers. “Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.” Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials. The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said. Uses different tactics Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to. “ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.” Companies need a secure fallback Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well. “The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.” Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders. “When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.” HR systems a prize Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable. “HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.” His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

items.title: Closing the Process-to-Packet Chasm: Why We Built Zscaler Endpoint Context (And Why Your EDR Loves It)
items.summary: If you have ever spent a Tuesday afternoon in a Security Operations Center (SOC), you have watched the most expensive game of "telephone" in enterprise IT.It starts with a network alert. An outbound encrypted connection to an unfamiliar IP address or a newly registered domain. The SOC analyst looks at the alert and asks a deceptively simple question: What on the user’s machine actually opened this connection?Was it a legitimate Chrome browser tab? A developer’s CLI utility? A rogue GenAI desktop agent? Or was it powershell.exe spawned by a malicious ClickFix lure, quietly beaconing out to a Cobalt Strike command-and-control (C2) server?Historically, the network couldn't tell you. A network proxy sees packets, TLS handshakes, and IP headers. The network doesn’t see Process IDs (PIDs), parent execution paths, or unsigned binaries. items.summary: The recent cyberattack on French refrigerators and our tracking of the malicious AI framework ARTEX show that threat actors are increasingly using AI to accelerate attacks, expand their reach, and improve their effectiveness. GreenJuliett, the group behind operational technology (OT) cyberattacks similar to those in France, has begun incorporating AI into its OT attack chain. Understanding the scale AI offers financially motivated and state-sponsored threat actors helps us see it as more than a tool: it’s something that can fill an operator’s role, even while humans remain in control. On October 11 and 12, 2026, someone changed the defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at more than 700 retail locations in France. This resulted in fires, damaged equipment, and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting the physical impacts of attacks against operational technology (OT). On November 9, France attributed the attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). We track activity that likely belongs to an element of Shahid Kaveh as GreenJuliett. GreenJuliett (also known as CyberAv3ngers and Bauxite) builds infrastructure aimed at internet-facing PLCs. And while that work continued through at least October 30, despite repeated public reporting on the group, the target set began to widen. Between August and October, we observed GreenJuliett-linked infrastructure scanning, or attempting to exploit, Fortinet FortiGate firewalls, edge devices that protect OT networks, in Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Our network data suggests the group is also working to add internet-of-things (IoT) and CCTV devices to its list. While we have not independently tied GreenJuliett infrastructure to the refrigeration attacks, over the past three months, we have seen the group continue to target PLCs (programmable logic controllers), which are similar to the internet-exposed controllers the refrigerators in France used. We have also observed that AI is now part of how they work. From Accounts to Infrastructure In October 2024, OpenAI banned accounts it assessed as belonging to CyberAv3ngers. The operators had used ChatGPT to research default credentials for PLCs, compile lists of electricity companies and common PLCs in Jordan, and draft scripts against industrial protocols (such as Modbus TCP, a control protocol that allows PLCs to communicate quickly on local networks). However, in 2026, the picture is different. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude. While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude.

While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment.
